analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security taxes on high earners to fund higher benefits for low-paid and long-retired beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced in January 2023 until a December 2024 subcommittee referral, and the 118th Congress ended without floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the Social Security payroll tax gradually from 6.2% to 6.5% for both workers and employers, and phase out the cap on earnings subject to the tax, so that high earners pay Social Security tax on income above roughly $160,000. The new revenue funds benefit increases: a minimum benefit pegged to the poverty line for people who worked many years at low wages, a gradually larger bonus for people who draw benefits for many years, and continuation of child benefits through age 26 for full-time students.
analysis.who_benefits: Lifetime low earners, who would be guaranteed a benefit at least at the poverty line after a long career; people who draw Social Security for 16 or more years, whose checks would grow by up to 5% a year to keep up with a long retirement; and children of retired, disabled, or deceased workers in college, whose benefits would continue through age 26. The program's trust fund also gains revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low earners, long-retired beneficiaries, and students

how_it_helps.text: Sets a new minimum benefit so a worker with 30 or more years in the workforce cannot receive less than the federal poverty guideline, with a lower percentage for shorter careers and credit for up to 5 years spent caring for young children.
Adds a benefit increase for beneficiaries who have been on the rolls 16 years or longer, rising to 5% of the benefit at 20 years, to protect people whose fixed checks wear thin over long retirements.
Extends child benefits for full-time post-secondary students from age 19 to age 26, continuing survivor and disability benefits through college.
Phases out the taxable earnings cap over about a decade and raises the payroll tax rate to 6.5% by 2029, directing the new revenue to benefits and to the program's financing.
Provides that the benefit increases would not count as income for Medicaid and other means-tested programs, so beneficiaries would not lose other aid.

analysis.who_pays: The tax increase falls hardest on high earners: the payroll tax rate rises for every covered worker and employer by 0.3 percentage points over six years, and the cap on taxable earnings phases out, so wages above roughly $160,000 become taxable. Self-employed people with high earnings pay the full combined increase, and employers pay a matching share on high salaries, which could pressure wage growth. High earners would receive a new 3% benefit factor on the newly taxed earnings above the old cap, but far less than they pay in.

drawbacks.text: The rate increase applies to all covered workers and employers, not only to earnings above the cap: employee and employer rates each rise from 6.2% to 6.5% by 2029, and the self-employment rate rises from 12.4% to 13%.

Phasing out the earnings cap raises the tax burden on high-income households and on owners of businesses with high self-employment income during their peak-earning years, and economists generally expect part of the employer-side increase to show up as slower wage growth.
Earnings above the old cap would earn only a 3% benefit factor, so some of the new revenue goes back out as benefits to affluent retirees rather than entirely to low-income beneficiaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is well targeted: a poverty-level floor for career low earners and extra support for very long retirements address the most serious gaps in Social Security, and the new 3% benefit factor on high earnings softens the fairness objection that high earners would pay without receiving anything. The cost is a genuine tax increase, spread broadly as a small rate rise and concentrated on six-figure earners through the cap phase-out, with employers paying a matching share. It is a conventional, straightforwardly designed expansion-and-solvency bill rather than a gimmick, but whether the tax increase is worth it is a real values question the bill never got to face on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, sat there for nearly two years, was sent to the Social Security subcommittee in a December 2024 lame-duck session, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Gwen Moore of Wisconsin introduced the bill on January 31, 2023, together with Rep. Jan Schakowsky, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The committee took no action on the bill for nearly two years; on December 17, 2024, near the end of the Congress, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security.
The bill had two cosponsors, both Democrats, and never received a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the Social Security wage cap and their employers are better off because the bill died: they keep today's 6.2% rate and the earnings cap, and no low-income beneficiary sees an increase.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the wage cap

for.name: Rep. Gwen Moore
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered two cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's original co-sponsor at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during nearly two years in which it sat in the committee; it went only to a subcommittee in the final weeks of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both cosponsors were Democrats and the bill drew no Republican support; the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee took no action on it.

industries.industry: High earners above the Social Security wage cap
industries.note: They would pay Social Security tax on earnings above roughly $160,000 plus a higher rate on all earnings, receiving only a 3% benefit factor on the newly taxed income. Blocking the bill preserved the current cap.

Employers would pay a matching 0.3-point rate increase on payroll, including on high salaries. The cost is modest per worker but rises with the wage bill, and part of it is generally expected to fall on wages.

industries.industry: Self-employed professionals and business owners with high incomes
industries.note: They would pay the full combined rate increase, from 12.4% to 13%, plus tax on self-employment income above the phased-out cap, with no employer to share the cost.
